content: This page provides a detailed explanation of edit conflicts and the methods to address them effectively. To understand an edit conflict, consider the following scenario: Alice clicks Edit this page on a specific page. Bob also clicks Edit this page on the same page. Alice completes her edits and clicks Save page, saving her version of the page. Bob then finishes his edits and clicks Save page, but instead of saving, he encounters an edit conflict page. Layout of the Edit Conflict Page At the top of the edit conflict page, Alice's version of the entire page is displayed, even if Bob was editing only a specific section. At the bottom, the text Bob was about to submit is shown. This could either be Bob's version of the entire page (if he edited the whole page) or just the section he was working on. In the middle, a diff comparison is presented, showing the differences between Alice's and Bob's edits. For the section Bob was editing, the diff highlights both his changes and Alice's changes, excluding any identical modifications. For other sections, the diff displays the full new text as if all of it were added. Bob can edit the upper text and press Save. If Bob was editing a section, this will be interpreted as the new version of that section. However, this may inadvertently duplicate other sections unless Bob deletes them before saving. This behavior appears to be a bug. In cases where the system is slow, pressing Save multiple times before the system responds can result in an edit conflict with oneself. The system recognizes the earlier change but has not yet processed it. While viewing the edit conflict page, the first change may be processed in the background, causing the upper text to no longer reflect the current version. The diff then shows a combined edit, and for section editing, it may display the addition of other sections. Resolving an Edit Conflict If Bob made minor changes while Alice made significant ones, Bob might choose to work from Alice's version and re-merge his changes. He could add a note like via edit conflict to alert Alice and others that he had to merge his edits, allowing Alice to review the changes for accuracy. If Bob made substantial changes and Alice made minor ones, Bob might prefer to work from his version. In this case, Bob can copy the bottom text into the top text (or just the relevant section) with an appropriate edit summary, such as via edit conflict, will re-merge. Bob can then review the page history, identify Alice's changes, and reapply them to his version in a separate edit. If both Alice and Bob made significant changes, resolving the conflict becomes more complex. For instance, if both added large sections on the same topic, it might be best for Bob to submit his changes and then collaborate with Alice to review both versions and decide which is better. Bob should not overwrite Alice's changes without consideration. Good faith is assumed, and mistakes are occasionally made, especially by newcomers who may not fully understand the edit conflict process. However, Bob must not routinely ignore edit conflicts or overwrite Alice's work out of laziness. Contributors are encouraged to double-check their merges using the diff feature. Logical Edit Conflicts Logical edit conflicts occur when two editors make changes that are incompatible but not detected by the system as an edit conflict. For example, if someone copies the entire text of a page, makes changes offline, and then pastes it back as a single new edit, any changes made by others in the meantime may be lost. To avoid this, editors should either paste only into the same edit box they originally copied from or check the page history for intervening edits and merge those changes before pasting back. Mistakes Mistakes can occur during the merging process because editors are human. This may result in some of Alice's changes being accidentally reversed. Logical edit conflicts are not always immediately visible. Sometimes, Bob may have valid reasons to think Alice's changes are not useful. In such cases, Alice and Bob are expected to resolve their differences amicably. If Alice made a minor change that Bob accidentally reversed, Alice should not revert to her version. It is unacceptable for Alice to undo Bob's major improvements to protect her minor edits or to punish Bob for his carelessness. If the page has since been edited by others, such as Sarah and Jonathan, Alice should edit Bob's version, reinstate her minor improvements, and leave Bob's major improvements intact. She may add an edit summary, such as Reinstating link which Bob accidentally removed. If Bob repeats his error, Alice should have a friendly discussion on his talk page, point him to this page, and ask him to be more careful in the future. This is particularly important for newcomers, though even experienced users may occasionally need a reminder. Prevention To reduce the likelihood of edit conflicts, you can adjust your editing habits. For example, focus on editing pages that have not been recently modified, such as those listed on ancient pages. Another strategy is to make a single larger change rather than frequent smaller ones. While this increases the chance of encountering an edit conflict, it reduces the likelihood of causing conflicts for others. Using the Show preview button can also help. Wikipedia provides an In Use notice in its Template namespace to signal that a page is being edited over a long period. Simply add `{{inuse}}` to an article before starting a major edit and remove the template when finished. Conclusion Edit conflicts can be frustrating and time-consuming, but they are an inevitable part of collaborative editing. By understanding the process, resolving conflicts amicably, and adopting preventive measures, contributors can minimize disruptions and maintain a productive editing environment.
